panels.rationale: Coronal contrast CT from a real patient in a case report of retroperitoneal fibrosis following etanercept. The caption and in-text explicitly attribute the scan to retroperitoneal fibrosis, showing the classic periaortic/infra-renal fibrotic soft-tissue encasement with bilateral ureteric involvement and right-sided hydroureteronephrosis, matching the configured target disease.
panels.attribution_text: Goh et al. Retroperitoneal Fibrosis following Etanercept for Ankylosing Spondylitis.. Mediterranean journal of rheumatology 2026. doi:10.31138/mjr.181025.erf. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Computer Topography (CT) scan demonstrating retroperitoneal fibrosis.
in_text_mentions: After seven years of etanercept therapy, the patient presented with recurrent episodes of lower back pain over a 12-month period. Initial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) findings were suggestive of disc degeneration as the underlying cause. However, she subsequently developed bilateral loin pain, and a computed tomography (CT) scan revealed retroperitoneal soft-tissue thickening encasing the infra-renal abdominal aorta, accompanied by moderate right-sided hydroureteronephrosis (Figure 1).

white arrow: left internal iliac artery involvement; abnormal vessel FDG uptake differentiated from physiological urinary tract uptake (black arrows) using co-registered CECT

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Axial CECT from a patient in an IgG4-related aortitis/periaortitis (retroperitoneal fibrosis spectrum) study shows perivascular soft-tissue thickening at the left internal iliac artery (white arrow), corresponding to iliac vessel encasement by retroperitoneal fibrosis. It is a real human-patient image of the configured target disease; no other disease, control, or diagram is shown. b: Fused FDG-PET/CT at the same axial level demonstrates focal abnormal FDG uptake in the left internal iliac artery wall (white arrow), representing active perivascular inflammation within the IgG4-related periaortitis/retroperitoneal fibrosis spectrum. Black arrows indicate physiological urinary-tract uptake that PET/CT alone cannot separate from disease, but the panel is not a normal or control image; the abnormal vascular uptake is explicitly supported by the caption and in-text.

Axial (a) and coronal (b and c) non-contrast CT KUB images demonstrating bilateral hydroureteronephrosis (blue arrows) with an associated lobulated retroperitoneal soft-tissue mass encasing the abdominal aorta, inferior vena cava, and bilateral ureters (yellow arrows), consistent with retroperitoneal fibrosis. CT KUB: Computed tomography of kidneys, ureters and bladder
in_text_mentions: e acute kidney injury, with a serum creatinine of 10.30 mg/dL on admission, rising to 11.00 mg/dL on 13 July 2025. Routine laboratory investigations are summarized in Table 1. A non-contrast computed tomography of kidneys, ureters, and bladder (CT KUB) performed on 12 July 2025 revealed a lobulated retroperitoneal soft-tissue mass encasing the abdominal aorta, inferior vena cava, and bilateral ureters, with associated bilateral hydroureteronephrosis (Figure 1). These findings were consistent with retroperitoneal fibrosis and correlated with the patient’s obstructive uropathy and renal failure.

in_text_mentions: month ago, an urgent unenhanced computed tomography scan of the kidneys, ureters, and bladder (CT KUB) was performed, which showed a large lobulated soft tissue mass seen superiorly at about the level of the distal abdominal aortic bifurcation and extending inferiorly and posteriorly into the deep pelvis to below the sacroiliac joints (Figure 1). The left kidney was smaller in size and hydronephrotic (grade 3), with obstruction likely at the proximal ureter, while the right kidney was of normal size with grade 1 hydronephrosis (Figure 3). There was no evidence of left renal or ureteric stone.

The patient was discussed at the urology multi-disciplinary team (MDT) meeting on account of his poor kidney function despite left ureteric stent in situ and admitting scan findings. A review of previous unenhanced computed tomography scans of kidneys, ureters, and bladder showed bilateral hydronephrosis (Figure 3), and the recommendation was for bilateral ureteric double J stent insertion, and subsequent computed tomography (CT) guided biopsy of the retroperitoneal mass in the future; his kidney function had not improved sufficiently to arrange a contrast-enhanced computed tomography scan.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Axial nonenhanced CT captioned as RPF before treatment shows an irregular isoattenuating retroperitoneal mass (arrow) anterior to the lower abdominal aorta, a classic periaortic fibrotic plaque of retroperitoneal fibrosis; the disease-focused article title (IgG4-related retroperitoneal fibrosis) supports the IgG4-related subtype. [raw subtype: IgG4-related] B: Second axial nonenhanced CT slice of the same pre-treatment RPF study shows the irregular isoattenuating retroperitoneal mass (arrow) extending lateral to the iliac arteries, consistent with periaortic fibrotic plaque with iliac vessel involvement in retroperitoneal fibrosis. [raw subtype: IgG4-related] C: Contrast-enhanced CT shows left hydronephrosis with delayed renal contrast excretion (arrow) due to distal ureteral encasement by the RPF mass, a classic obstructive complication of retroperitoneal fibrosis explicitly captioned as such. [raw subtype: IgG4-related]

panels.figure_caption: Contrast-enhanced CT of RPF before treatment. (A, B) Axial nonenhanced CT images show an irregular retroperitoneal mass (arrow) which is isoattenuating to muscle. The mass is located anterior and lateral to the lower abdominal aorta and iliac arteries. (C) Left hydronephrosis is secondary to distal encasement of the ureter by the mass. The renal excretion of contrast material was delayed (arrow). CT = computed tomography, RPF = retroperitoneal fibrosis.
in_text_mentions: Radiographs of the chest were unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced abdominal computed tomography (CT) revealed left hydronephrosis and a periaortic mass (Fig. 1). The mass surrounding the aorta appeared to be soft tissue rather than lymph nodes or tumor, suggesting left ureteral stenosis due to RPF, leading to hydronephrosis of the left kidney. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) revealed no significant dilation of the common bile duct or the extra- and intra-hepatic bile ducts.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Axial contrast CT of the abdomen/pelvis in a patient with idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis; the red arrow indicates a periaortic retroperitoneal fibrotic plaque encasing the aorta and common iliac vessels, a textbook CT manifestation of the target disease. B: Coronal contrast CT of the abdomen/pelvis in the same patient; the red arrow indicates left ureteral obstruction with proximal hydronephrosis, a classic complication of retroperitoneal fibrosis and a direct manifestation of the target disease.
panels.attribution_text: Khalil et al. Unique Presentation of Idiopathic Retroperitoneal Fibrosis in a Primary Care Setting.. Cureus 2021. doi:10.7759/cureus.18429. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast. The red arrow in A shows retroperitoneal fibrosis surrounding the descending vessels originating from the abdominal aorta. The red arrow in B shows left ureteral hydronephrosis before stent placement. CT: computed tomography
in_text_mentions: diagnostic imaging, a 2 L bolus of normal saline fluid was administered intravenously followed by maintenance fluid. CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast was significant for RPF, periaortitis involving the distal aorta and its bilateral common iliac arteries, decreased perfusion of the left kidney with mild hydronephrosis, and obstruction of a portion of the left distal ureter (Figure 1). A high-resolution chest CT scan reported multiple small areas of clustered cystic and/or emphysematous changes scattered throughout the lungs and a few ground-glass nodules in the right lung apex.

plate_findings.evidence: left caliceal, pelvic, and ureteral dilatation (arrow in A); modest dilatation of the calyceal cavities and the renal pelvis, as well as of the proximal tract of the ureter in the absence of definite images suggestive of lithiasis

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Panel A is an axial abdominal CT from a patient with retroperitoneal fibrosis showing left hydroureteronephrosis and perirenal fascia thickening, supporting the target disease. B: Panel B is an axial abdominal CT from a patient with retroperitoneal fibrosis showing right renal pelvic/ureteral dilatation, medialized swollen right kidney, and perirenal/pararenal fascial changes, supporting the target disease.
panels.attribution_text: Gagliardi et al. Retroperitoneal Fibrosis: A Puzzle of Elusive Causal Link.. Cureus 2024. doi:10.7759/cureus.56220. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: CT abdomen: left caliceal, pelvic, and ureteral dilatation (arrow in A) and right kidney medialized and swollen (arrow in B). There is modest dilatation of the calyceal cavities and the renal pelvis, as well as of the proximal tract of the ureter in the absence of definite images suggestive of lithiasis. Minimal thickening of the perirenal fascia is also associated (A). Diffuse heterogeneity of mesenteric adipose tissue, right kidney slightly medialized, increased in size with a swollen appearance, modest dilatation of the calyceal cavities and the right renal pelvis as well as of the proximal tract of the ureter. Thickening of the perirenal fascia is associated with heterogeneity of the anterior and posterior pararenal spaces (B).
in_text_mentions: Abdominal CT scan revealed diffuse mesenteric adipose tissue heterogeneity, medialization of the right kidney with increased size and swelling, and moderate dilation of the calyceal cavities, pelvis, and proximal segments of the ureters. Additionally, it detected thickening of the perirenal fascia with heterogeneity of the anterior and posterior pararenal spaces and thickening of adipose tissue in the para-aortic and paracaval regions (Figure 1).

plate_findings.evidence: in-text: "remarkable storiform fibrosis mixed with fibroblasts, neutrophil granulocytes, plasma cells, and lymphocytes (Fig. 3A)"

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: H&E photomicrograph of the surgical specimen from a case explicitly labeled idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis; the caption and in-text describe storiform fibrosis with a mixed inflammatory cell infiltrate, directly matching the vocabulary finding for storiform collagenous fibrosis. Real human-patient histology showing a specific manifestation of the target disease. [raw subtype: idiopathic] B: Immunohistochemistry for vimentin performed on the same idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis surgical specimen shows the spindle stroma cells positive for vimentin, supporting the fibroblastic/myofibroblastic nature of the lesion. Real human-patient IHC of the target disease; vimentin positivity is clearly present but absent from the provided vocabulary, so it is recorded as a proposed finding rather than forced into an unrelated vocabulary key. [raw subtype: idiopathic]
panels.attribution_text: Yan et al. Idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis causing unilateral ureteral and sigmoid colon obstruction: A case report.. Medicine 2017. doi:10.1097/md.0000000000006105. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis. (A) Photomicrograph from the surgical specimen using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) (×200 magnification) showing mature fiber tissue mixed with fibroblasts, neutrophil granulocytes, plasma cells, and lymphocytes. (B) Immunohistochemistry for vimentin (×200 magnification) showing that the spindle stroma cells were positive for vimentin. H&E = hematoxylin and eosin.
in_text_mentions: The pathological diagnosis was idiopathic RPF. The fibrous component was interpreted as remarkable storiform fibrosis mixed with fibroblasts, neutrophil granulocytes, plasma cells, and lymphocytes (Fig. 3A). Immunohistochemistry showed that vimentin was positive (Fig. 3B), smooth muscle actin was partially positive, β-catenin was positive (cell membrane and cytoplasm), Ki-67 was very weakly positive (<1%), GIST-1 was equivocal, and desmin, CD30, anaplastic lymphoma kinase, CD117, CD34, α-inhibin, S-100, epithelial membrane antigen, and cytokeratin pan were all negative.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Real patient H&E histopathology from a case report of isolated IgG4-related retroperitoneal fibrosis. Caption and in-text directly describe dense collagen fibers with dense mixed chronic inflammation and widespread obliterative endophlebitis, which are classic histologic features of retroperitoneal fibrosis. Disease attribution is supported by the disease-focused article title and the specific captioned manifestation. [raw subtype: IgG4-related] B: Real patient IgG4 immunohistochemistry from the same case report of isolated IgG4-related retroperitoneal fibrosis. The caption explicitly states increased IgG4-positive plasma cells (>10/HPF, ~35/HPF), a hallmark of IgG4-related retroperitoneal fibrosis. Disease attribution is directly supported by the article title and the captioned immunostain manifestation. [raw subtype: IgG4-related]

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (RT, LT). RT: Real-patient abdominal ultrasound of the right kidney from a case report of retroperitoneal fibrosis; caption documents bilateral hydronephrosis with slightly increased cortical echogenicity, matching the vocabulary finding retroperitoneal_fibrosis_obstructive_hydronephrosis; the disease-focused article title attributes the hydronephrosis to retroperitoneal fibrosis. LT: Real-patient abdominal ultrasound of the left kidney from a case report of retroperitoneal fibrosis; caption documents bilateral hydronephrosis with slightly increased cortical echogenicity, matching the vocabulary finding retroperitoneal_fibrosis_obstructive_hydronephrosis; the disease-focused article title attributes the hydronephrosis to retroperitoneal fibrosis.

in_text_mentions: On Day 1, a 56-year-old woman presented to a nephrologist with complaints of generalized edema and decreased urine output that had begun 7 days prior. She also reported nausea following the reduction in urine output, along with a loss of appetite. Renal ultrasound revealed bilateral hydronephrosis and slightly increased echogenicity in both kidneys (Fig. 1). She had no significant past medical or family history.

panels.rationale: Single axial contrast-enhanced abdominal CT from a human patient. Caption and in-text explicitly attribute the findings to early idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis: mild periureteric fibrotic changes with mild bilateral hydroureteronephrosis/retroperitoneal fat stranding. The obstructive hydronephrosis finding is directly supported by caption and in-text; periureteric fibrotic changes and fat stranding are stated but absent from the vocabulary, so they are proposed. No skin, no stated ethnicity, no annotations; age not stated.
panels.attribution_text: Ali et al. Idiopathic Retroperitoneal Fibrosis: An East African Diagnostic Challenge.. Cureus 2021. doi:10.7759/cureus.15683. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Axial enhanced CT showing mild periureteric fibrotic changes and mild hydronephrosis.
in_text_mentions: ticular ultrasound done was reported as normal with incidental finding of right inguinal lymphadenopathy. An abdominal CT scan showed mild splenomegaly with mild bilateral hydroureteronephrosis with retroperitoneal fat stranding suggestive of early retroperitoneal fibrosis (Figure 1). An ultrasound of the liver showed a gall bladder that was of normal size and wall thickness, no dilatation of the intrahepatic bile ducts, and no calculi. A follow-up FibroScan showed no fibrosis. An MRI of the liver was also reported as normal. A liver biopsy showed mild non-alcoholic hepatitis, but no fibrosis.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 6 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F). A: Ultrasound shows a retroperitoneal mass consistent with retroperitoneal fibrosis, as described in the caption. B: Color Doppler ultrasound demonstrates minimal vascularity within the retroperitoneal mass, supporting a fibrotic etiology. C: CT scan shows a retroperitoneal mass with no significant enhancement, typical of retroperitoneal fibrosis. D: Enhanced CT demonstrates a large retroperitoneal mass consistent with retroperitoneal fibrosis. E: Enhanced CT shows a retroperitoneal mass consistent with retroperitoneal fibrosis. F: PET-CT shows mildly increased FDG uptake in the retroperitoneal mass, consistent with inflammation or fibrosis.
panels.attribution_text: Cheng et al. Systemic lupus erythematosus complicated by retroperitoneal fibrosis: A case report and literature review.. Medicine 2025. doi:10.1097/md.0000000000041208. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Imaging features of a 32-year-old woman with a retroperitoneal mass (A and B) Ultrasound revealed multiple hypoechoic nodules in the retroperitoneal area, with indistinct borders and an irregular echo pattern. CDFI showed minimal blood flow, suggesting a fibrotic nature of the mass. (C–E) CT scan demonstrated a retroperitoneal mass with a shadow. The 3-phase enhancement did not show any significant increase in intensity, indicating a nonmalignant lesion. (F) PET-CT showed patchy hyperdensity in the retroperitoneal space, with slightly increased FDG metabolism diffusely, suggesting inflammation or fibrosis rather than malignancy. Clinical significance: The imaging features, including ultrasound, CT, and PET-CT findings, assist in differentiating RPF from other retroperitoneal pathologies, such as malignancies. The absence of significant enhancement on CT and the lack of increased FDG uptake on PET-CT support a diagnosis of RPF rather than cancer. CDFI = Color Doppler flow imaging, CT = computer tomography, PET-CT = positron emission tomography-computed tomography, RPF = retroperitoneal fibrosis.
in_text_mentions: One year prior: the patient presented to our hospital with transient lumbar soreness. Imaging studies revealed a retroperitoneal mass (ultrasound: Fig. 1A and B; magnetic resonance imaging (MRI): Fig. 2A–C). The mass demonstrated delayed enhancement, suggestive of RPF or lymphoma. PET-CT indicated mildly increased metabolic activity (Fig. 1F). The patient declined further evaluation and hospitalization.

On June 13, 2022, the patient was readmitted to the emergency department after another episode of syncope. Laboratory tests revealed severe pancytopenia, hypoalbuminemia, and active lupus (immunological findings are detailed in Table 1). Imaging studies showed a significant increase in the size of the retroperitoneal mass, accompanied by massive ascites (enhanced CT: Figs. 1C–E).An ultrasound-guided biopsy confirmed RPF, with negative immunohistochemical staining for IgG and IgG4 (Fig. 3A and B).

in_text_mentions: Differential diagnosis of pancreatic cancer, tuberculosis, and lymphoma were made. To make the exact diagnosis, an EUS-guided biopsy of the pancreatic mass was obtained, which showed fragments of benign biliary epithelium with mild lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate (containing plasma cells), dense fibrosis, and background hemorrhage. The findings of the biopsy were consistent with IgG4-related RF. On immunohistochemistry, IgG4, CD138, and MUM-1 highlighted plasma cells with only a few cells positive for CD20 (Figure 2).

panels.rationale: Single axial contrast-enhanced CT image of the abdomen from a case series of retroperitoneal fibrosis. Caption explicitly identifies the urorenal subtype of retroperitoneal fibrosis with bilateral hydronephrosis and inflammatory tissue involving the ureter; the image visibly shows a dilated right renal collecting system (hydronephrosis) and periaortic/periureteral inflammatory soft tissue encasing and displacing the ureters medially. This is a real human-patient image with a specific manifestation of the configured target disease, so it qualifies for the library. [raw subtype: urorenal]

in_text_mentions: As there are no radiological, microbiological, or biochemical methods that would uniquely differentiate between primary and secondary fibrosis, at first, we tried to exclude secondary causes, especially malignancies. We performed a series of diagnostic tests, both biochemical and imaging (CT, MRI) or endoscopic, and found that all of the cases were primary RPF. Figure 1 presents vascular and Figure 2 urorenal subtype.

panels.figure_caption: Histopathologic features of IgG4-related retroperitoneal fibrosis. (A) Haematoxylin and eosin (H&E, ×4) image demonstrates dense fibrosis with infiltrative extension into the adjacent perirenal fat. (B) H&E (×10) image shows a characteristic storiform fibrotic pattern. (C) Orcein stain (×40) highlights obliterative phlebitis within the fibroinflammatory tissue. (D) H&E (×40) image reveals a dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate. (E) Immunohistochemistry (×40) demonstrates numerous IgG-positive plasma cells. (F) Immunohistochemistry (×40) shows abundant IgG4-positive plasma cells (up to 200 IgG4-positive cells per high-power field; IgG4/IgG ratio 200/220), supporting the diagnosis of IgG4-related disease.
in_text_mentions: Gross examination (Figure 2) of the nephrectomy specimen demonstrated a single ovoid mass confined within the kidney, with an intact but thickened renal capsule and adjacent fibrotic tissue. Microscopic evaluation (Figure 3) confirmed clear cell RCC, grade 2, confined to the kidney (pT1b), with no perinephric fat invasion, no lymphovascular invasion, and negative surgical margins.

panels.figure_caption: Retroperitoneal biopsy findings. A: Hematoxylin and eosin staining showing fibrous proliferation with hyalinized collagen, focally-forming storiform fascicles, dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate (yellow arrowhead) with occasional germinal centers. Black arrowheads showing the normal retroperitoneal fibro-adipose tissue. B: High-power field showing classical plasma cell (white arrowhead) within the infiltrate; immunohistochemical staining assessment of the IgG4/IgG ratio performed by quantification of stained cells, showing IgG-positive lymphocytes and plasma cells of 60 – 70/high-power field (C), and IgG4-positive lymphocytes and plasma cells of 30/high-power field (D), demonstrating an IgG4/IgG ratio of 42 – 50%.
in_text_mentions: d lysis of extensive bowel adhesions. During the procedure, the retroperitoneal soft tissue density was biopsied, which revealed fibrous proliferation with hyalinized collagen, focally-forming storiform fascicles, dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate with occasional germinal centers (Figure 2A, B), and focal obliterative phlebitis. Immunohistochemical staining revealed IgG4-positive plasma cells (60 – 70/high-power field), and the IgG4/IgG plasma cell ratio was > 40% (Figure 2C, D), in support of a diagnosis of IgG4-RD. Following the procedure, the serum creatinine dropped from 4.8 to 1.8 mg/dL.

panels.rationale: High-power H&E section from the CT-guided transgluteal biopsy of the retroperitoneal mass in a case of IgG4-related retroperitoneal fibrosis. The image shows dense collagenous fibrosis with a rich inflammatory infiltrate (macrophages, plasma cells, lymphocytes) and fat obliteration with a single remaining adipocyte (black arrow), matching the in-text description of storiform fibrosis obliterating fat. Real patient diagnostic histology, clearly attributable to retroperitoneal fibrosis (IgG4-related subtype per article title and in-text). Plasma cell infiltrate is captioned and the IgG4 association is explicitly supported by the in-text biopsy interpretation; no finding claims exceed the captioned/visual evidence. panels.figure_caption: Pathological findings of retroperitoneal tissue (a, b: hematoxylin and eosin staining). Microscopic examination revealed lymphocytic infiltration with layered fibrosis (a: 40×, b: 400×) (c: immunohistochemistry [IHC] for IgG). IHC staining demonstrated the presence of IgG‐positive plasma cells (×100) (d: IHC for IgG4). IHC staining revealed the presence of numerous IgG4‐positive plasma cells. The number of IgG4‐positive cells corresponded to approximately 70% of the total number of IgG‐positive cells in the same area (100×) (e: IHC for CD3, f: IHC for CD20). Immunohistochemistry demonstrated that lymphocytes were positive for both CD3 (e: ×100) and CD20 (f: ×100), suggesting an association with both T and B cell lymphocytes (g: IHC for CD4, h: IHC for CD8). T cell lymphocytes infiltrating the lesion were positive for both CD4 and CD8 with a predominance of CD8.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: H&E omental biopsy section showing perivascular inflammation, part of the captioned 'spectrum of vasculitic changes' in this ergotamine-induced retroperitoneal fibrosis case. Disease attribution rests on the disease-focused article title plus the specific captioned manifestation in this patient's biopsy. Perivascular inflammation is non-specific and has no vocabulary finding key, so it is proposed; confidence is moderate. B: H&E omental biopsy showing lymphocytic phlebitis with venular wall infiltration by lymphoid cells (yellow arrow), mapping to the vocabulary's obliterative phlebitis histology finding for retroperitoneal fibrosis. The caption notes the plasma cells were IgG4-negative, so the IgG4 plasma cell infiltrate finding is deliberately not tagged. Phlebitis is a recognized histologic feature of retroperitoneal fibrosis, supporting classic typicality. C: H&E inset showing circumferential perivenular lymphoplasmacytic...

in_text_mentions: segment of circumferential, hypodense, mildly enhancing soft tissue mass with an infiltrative and spiculated appearance in the retroperitoneum, completely encasing the infrarenal aorta and inferior vena cava (IVC), extending along the proximal portions of the common iliac arteries without ureteric involvement (Figure 3a and 3b). Following the initiation of corticosteroid therapy, the symptoms improved over time and the patient is currently under follow-up.

in_text_mentions: A 54-year-old man presented to our department with a 2-month history of back pain and painful urination. A contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) revealed a large retroperitoneal soft tissue mass encircling the abdominal aorta, surrounding vessels, and the right ureter ( Fig. 1 ). He had an average leukocyte level (7300/µL), within the normal range for tumor markers and IgG4 levels, and a C-reactive protein level of 38.88 mg/L. The clinical picture was highly suggestive of retroperitoneal fibrosis (RPF); however, for a definite diagnosis, a biopsy of the lesion was necessary.

plate_findings.evidence: Peri-aortic soft tissue enhancement of 10 mm

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Axial arterial-phase CTA from an RPF patient showing peri-aortic soft tissue encasement of the abdominal aorta, measured at 10 mm. The article title and in-text context confirm retroperitoneal fibrosis, and the peri-aortic soft tissue is the classic CT manifestation of RPF. Measurement calipers (10 mm) are annotated on the image. B: Axial arterial-phase CTA from the same RPF patient showing the combined aortic and peri-aortic soft tissue enhancement measured at 30 mm. The peri-aortic soft tissue component is directly visible and captioned, representing the classic periaortic fibrotic plaque of retroperitoneal fibrosis. Measurement calipers (30 mm) are annotated on the image.
panels.attribution_text: Sultan et al. Management of retroperitoneal fibrosis with endovascular aneurysm repair in patients refractory to medical management.. Frontiers in surgery 2022. doi:10.3389/fsurg.2022.946675. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Computed tomography angiography (CTA) images illustrating the determination of the aortic retroperitoneal fibrosis index (peri-aortic soft tissue enhancement over maximum aortic diameter). (A) Peri-aortic soft tissue enhancement of 10 mm. (B) overall aortic enhancement of 30 mm, including the peri-aortic soft tissue enhancement.
in_text_mentions: tic soft tissue diameter relative to maximum aortic diameter. These measurements were taken after defining the aortic centre-line on arterial phase images. Aortic RPF index is zero for patients without RPF or any enhancement of peri-aortic soft tissue. Furthermore, we approximate the cross-sectional area of the peri-aortic soft tissue enhancements by using the formula π (Pi) times the radius squared (π * r2) (cross-sectional area of periaortic soft tissue enhancement = cross sectional area of the total aortic enhancement including aorta - cross sectional area surface area of aorta) (Figure 2).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: T1-weighted contrast-enhanced MRI panel shows the periaortic retroperitoneal fibro-inflammatory cuff involving the left common iliac artery root, consistent with retroperitoneal fibrosis. B: T2-weighted MRI panel shows intermediate-to-high signal periaortic cuff with arrowed active inflammation, matching active retroperitoneal fibrosis involving the left common iliac artery root.
panels.attribution_text: Gagliardi et al. Retroperitoneal Fibrosis: A Puzzle of Elusive Causal Link.. Cureus 2024. doi:10.7759/cureus.56220. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: MRI abdomen with contrast enhancement: periaortic thickness (arrow in A) with sign of inflammation/activity (arrow in B). Thickening of the adipose tissue in the peri-aortic area, forming a "cuff," with a maximum sub-centimeter thickness, extending along the sub-renal abdominal aorta to the carrefour, involving the root of the left common iliac artery. Signal characteristics are low on T1-weighted images (A) and intermediate to high on T2-weighted images (B), consistent with inflammatory/active tissue characteristics. Millimetric lymph node formations are present in the common iliac area, showing restricted diffusivity.
in_text_mentions: For a better characterization of the thickening of the para-aortic adipose tissue, an MRI was performed, confirming the thickening of the peri-aortic adipose tissue, sleeve-like, extending along the subrenal abdominal aorta to the common iliac artery root on the left. This thickening showed intermediate/high signal intensity on T2 and low signal intensity on T1, suggestive of inflammatory/active characteristics (Figure 3).

in_text_mentions: A 48-year-old male patient presented with no relevant history and a clinical picture of two months' evolution, characterized by a predominantly left abdominal pain, with the sensation of a mass. CT of the abdomen showed a retroperitoneal mass of infrarenal location, compromising the para-aortic, interaortocaval space in front of the aorta, extending to the aortoiliac bifurcation, with well-defined contours, surrounding the vascular structures without infiltrating them, 99 x 38 x 55 mm, and associated with left hydronephrosis (Figure 3). No distant involvement was evident.

in_text_mentions: A CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed mild left hydronephrosis and proximal hydroureter, but no calculus (Figure 1A). An ill-defined retroperitoneal soft tissue mass measuring 2.8 x 1.7 cm was seen along the anterior margin of the aorta and abutting the mid-segment of the left ureter (Figure 1B). She was also noted to have an ascending and descending thoracic aortic aneurysm (Figure 2A) and a proximal abdominal aortic aneurysm (Figure 2B). This was limited to the suprarenal abdominal aorta and the infrarenal part was normal in caliber.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Axial CT from a case of IgG4-related retroperitoneal fibrosis shows a heterogeneously enhancing soft tissue mass in the retroperitoneum abutting the superior mesenteric vein, consistent with retroperitoneal fibrosis. B: Sagittal CT demonstrates the retroperitoneal mass encasing the superior mesenteric artery with loss of fat planes and abutting the inferior vena cava, characteristic of retroperitoneal fibrosis. C: Coronal CT shows the retroperitoneal fibrotic mass encasing the left renal vein, a classic vascular encasement pattern of retroperitoneal fibrosis. D: Axial CT again shows the retroperitoneal soft tissue mass abutting the inferior vena cava posteriorly, supporting retroperitoneal fibrosis with IVC involvement.

panels.rationale: Single coronal PET-CT panel from a case report of periaortitis/retroperitoneal fibrosis in a patient with normal IgG4. The caption and in-text explicitly describe intense FDG uptake in the distal abdominal aortic wall with a surrounding soft-tissue sleeve extending below the bifurcation along the iliac arteries, plus aortic arch wall uptake — a direct, captioned manifestation of active periaortic/retroperitoneal fibrotic inflammation. It is a real human-patient image (prior triage: radiology, real patient, third-party false), not a diagram, control, or other-disease panel. Findings map to the vocabulary item retroperitoneal_fibrosis_retroperitoneal_fdg_uptake (FDG-avid periaortic fibrosis/active periaortic inflammation); the periaortic soft-tissue sleeve and aortic arch uptake are noted as proposed findings. No skin, ethnicity, or age stated; stage not applicable.
panels.attribution_text: Alarbi et al. Periaortitis and Retroperitoneal Fibrosis in a Patient With a Normal IgG4 Level: A Case Report and Review of the Literature.. Cureus 2026. doi:10.7759/cureus.114453. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: PET-CT scan (coronal plane) showing intense inhomogeneous FDG uptake in the aortic arch wall and intense homogeneous FDG uptake in the distal abdominal aortic wall and surrounding soft-tissue sleeve going below bifurcation level along the iliac arteries PET-CT: positron emission tomography-computed tomography, FDG: fluorodeoxyglucose.
in_text_mentions: neous fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) uptake along a 12-cm segment of the aortic arch wall. There was also intense, inhomogeneous FDG uptake in the distal abdominal aortic wall, with a surrounding soft-tissue sleeve extending below the aortic bifurcation along the iliac arteries for a total length of more than 20 cm. In addition, there was pathological FDG uptake in the wall of the splenic artery. No peripheral lesions amenable to biopsy were identified. The PET-CT findings supported an active inflammatory process involving the aortic wall at the aortic arch and distal abdominal aorta (Figures 3, 4).

panels.rationale: Single coronal contrast CT of a real patient (corroborated by caption-triage route 'keep'). The caption and in-text explicitly describe an enlarging retroperitoneal mass (7.6 x 3.8 x 5.6 cm, annotated 75.6 mm on the image) encasing the right ureter with mild right hydronephrosis, in an article titled 'Bilateral Hydronephrosis From Retroperitoneal Fibrosis.' This is a direct, specific manifestation of retroperitoneal fibrosis, so the panel is included. Only the captioned hydronephrosis is taken from the vocabulary; medial deviation, periaortic plaque, iliac/IVC involvement and FDG/MRI findings are not stated for this panel, so ureteral encasement is recorded as a proposed finding. No ethnicity, age or skin information is stated; typicality is classic for RPF with ureteral obstruction.

The in-text also notes right-sided hydronephrosis on the same CT workup, but this slice is below the renal hila and shows no collecting-system dilation, so only the periaortic fibrotic plaque is tagged. No ethnicity, age, or skin findings are stated or visible; no third-party copyright is indicated.

in_text_mentions: Approximately one month after the initial presentation, the patient was sent for a CT scan of his abdomen and pelvis (Figure 1), which revealed aortitis and retroperitoneal fibrosis. An inflammatory aortic aneurysm was seen with a thick peel and no saccular component. Follow-up labs shortly after his CT showed negative rheumatoid factor (RF), negative antinuclear antibodies (ANA), decrease in CRP to 10 mg/L, ESR to 27 mm/h, and ferritin to 425 ng/mL. The patient was subsequently evaluated by Vascular Surgery, at which time the patient reported no further weight loss and improvement of malaise

An MRI of the abdomen reaffirmed the presence of retroperitoneal fibrosis and bilateral ureteric stents and additionally demonstrated a fusiform aneurysm of the distal abdominal aorta (Figure 5).

in_text_mentions: A computed tomography (CT) scan of the kidneys, ureters, and bladder showed no urinary calculi. Subsequent CT angiography of the abdomen and pelvis revealed aortic mural thickening extending inferiorly from the level of the renal arteries, with areas of luminal narrowing and mild dilatation. Mildly enhancing soft-tissue density was also noted in the periaortic and retroperitoneal regions at the infrarenal level, suggestive of CP with associated retroperitoneal fibrosis (Figures 1, 2).

panels.rationale: Real patient sagittal fused PET-CT from a case report titled 'Periaortitis and Retroperitoneal Fibrosis...'. The caption and in-text describe an FDG-avid periaortic soft-tissue sleeve encasing the distal abdominal aorta and extending below the bifurcation along the iliac arteries, which is a direct imaging manifestation of active retroperitoneal fibrosis/periaortitis. Not a diagram, control, or other disease; attribution to retroperitoneal_fibrosis is supported by the disease-focused title and the specific captioned periaortic soft-tissue sleeve.
panels.attribution_text: Alarbi et al. Periaortitis and Retroperitoneal Fibrosis in a Patient With a Normal IgG4 Level: A Case Report and Review of the Literature.. Cureus 2026. doi:10.7759/cureus.114453. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 4.
panels.figure_caption: PET-CT scan (sagittal plane) showing intense inhomogeneous FDG uptake in the aortic arch wall and intense homogeneous FDG uptake in the distal abdominal aortic wall and surrounding soft-tissue sleeve going below bifurcation level along the iliac arteries
in_text_mentions: neous fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) uptake along a 12-cm segment of the aortic arch wall. There was also intense, inhomogeneous FDG uptake in the distal abdominal aortic wall, with a surrounding soft-tissue sleeve extending below the aortic bifurcation along the iliac arteries for a total length of more than 20 cm. In addition, there was pathological FDG uptake in the wall of the splenic artery. No peripheral lesions amenable to biopsy were identified. The PET-CT findings supported an active inflammatory process involving the aortic wall at the aortic arch and distal abdominal aorta (Figures 3, 4).

panels.rationale: H&E histopathology of a retroperitoneal mass biopsy from a patient with retroperitoneal fibrosis. The image shows characteristic features including storiform collagenous fibrosis, trapped adipose tissue, fibroblasts, and plasma cells (arrows). In-text confirms hypocellular fusocellular proliferation with vessel obliteration, consistent with retroperitoneal fibrosis.

in_text_mentions: tion, with a diameter greater than 4 cm, with no infiltration to the vessel wall and no evidence of distant involvement. The patient underwent laparotomy with findings of a retroperitoneal mass, attached to deep planes, which circumferentially involves the infrarenal abdominal aorta and the intrahepatic vena cava. An incisional biopsy was performed, given the unresectability of the lesion. Surgical pathology reported a hypocellular fusocellular proliferation without atypia, mitosis or necrosis, with trapped fat, with obliteration of vessels with abundant lymphocytes and plasmocytes (Figure 1).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Immunohistochemistry of retroperitoneal tissue from a human patient with retroperitoneal fibrosis (article title and in-text context) showing IgG-positive plasma cells infiltrating adipose tissue; brown DAB chromogen confirms IHC. IgG/IgG4 plasmocyte infiltrate is a classic histologic feature of IgG4-related retroperitoneal fibrosis. No age, ethnicity, or skin findings stated. [raw subtype: igg4_related] B: Immunohistochemistry of retroperitoneal adipose tissue from a human patient with retroperitoneal fibrosis showing IgG4-positive plasma cells (red chromogen; the caption's 'H&E 40X' label is inconsistent with the visible IHC staining pattern). IgG4-positive plasma cell infiltrate with >50 IgG4+ cells per high-power field is a classic histologic feature of IgG4-related retroperitoneal fibrosis. No age, ethnicity, or skin findings stated. [raw subtype: igg4_related]

in_text_mentions: month ago, an urgent unenhanced computed tomography scan of the kidneys, ureters, and bladder (CT KUB) was performed, which showed a large lobulated soft tissue mass seen superiorly at about the level of the distal abdominal aortic bifurcation and extending inferiorly and posteriorly into the deep pelvis to below the sacroiliac joints (Figure 1). panels.rationale: H&E histology from the index case's retroperitoneal mass biopsy, confirmed in text as idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis. The slide shows abundant dense collagenous (storiform/whorled) fibrosis replacing normal retroperitoneal soft tissue, the textbook histologic hallmark of RPF. IgG4-positive cells were explicitly non-diagnostic, so no IgG4-related subtype or IgG4 plasma cell finding is assigned. Red arrows annotate the fibrotic areas. [raw subtype: idiopathic]
panels.attribution_text: Okpii et al. Bilateral Ureteric Obstruction Due to Retroperitoneal Fibrosis: A Case Report.. Cureus 2022. doi:10.7759/cureus.28187. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Histology slide from biopsy of index case at 100um magnification showing abundant fibrosis (broken red lines) replacing normal retroperitoneal soft tissue
in_text_mentions: Further down his care, he had a core biopsy of the retroperitoneal mass which confirmed retroperitoneal fibrosis (Figure 2). The IgG4 positive cells were non-diagnostic of IgG4 disease, and mouse double minute 2 (MDM2) amplification using fluorescent in-situ hybridization (FISH) was negative, thus excluding possible sarcoma.

t of worsening dyselectrolytemia (severe hyperkalaemia, increasing creatinine) and poor urine output, which required continuous venovenous haemofiltration (CVVH) in the intensive care unit. He improved with CVVH and was transferred to a tertiary center, where he had a right nephrostomy inserted, and a biopsy of his retroperitoneal mass was done. The biopsy confirmed idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis (Figure 2) with IgG4 levels in the non-diagnostic range and negative FISH for MDM2 amplification. The patient was subsequently discharged with bilateral nephrostomies and ureteric stents in situ.

panels.rationale: Axial contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen from the article 'Retroperitoneal Fibrosis: Still a Diagnostic Challenge.' The red arrow points to retroperitoneal soft-tissue density in the periaortic region, and the caption explicitly identifies this as retroperitoneal fibrosis; in-text corroborates with retroperitoneal fat stranding extending through the abdomen and pelvis plus retroperitoneal lymph nodes. This is a real human-patient radiology image directly demonstrating the target disease, not a diagram, control, or other-disease panel, and not third-party material. No subtype (e.g., IgG4-related vs idiopathic) is specified in the caption, and no age or ethnicity is stated.

in_text_mentions: Given her chest pain and emesis, a chest X-ray was obtained to look for any signs of mediastinitis, but it was unremarkable. A contrast-enhanced abdominal computed tomography (CT) was performed to look for acute pancreatitis, which showed stranding within the retroperitoneal fat extending throughout the abdomen and pelvis, including the perirectal and presacral regions (Figure 1). Also, multiple small retroperitoneal lymph nodes and larger nodes in gastrohepatic, para-aortic, and aortocaval spaces were seen.

panels.rationale: Low-power H&E histology from aneurysm repair in a patient with bilateral hydronephrosis and clinical suspicion for idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis. The image shows the aortic wall with lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate in the tunica media and adventitia spilling into periaortic soft tissue, accompanied by collagenous fibrosis characteristic of retroperitoneal fibrosis. Disease attribution is supported by the article title and in-text mention of suspicion for idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis. Storiform fibrosis is assessed visually from the image; the prominent lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate is captured as a proposed finding since it lacks a direct vocabulary match for H&E periaortic inflammation.
panels.attribution_text: Sheth and Malik. Bilateral Hydronephrosis From Retroperitoneal Fibrosis.. Cureus 2020. doi:10.7759/cureus.12147. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 6.
panels.figure_caption: Low-power view of the aortic wall (tunica interna towards lower left corner) showing lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate in the tunica media and tunica adventitia, spilling into the periaortic soft tissue (H&E stain, 20x)
in_text_mentions: ociated chronic inflammatory cells. CD3 stain highlighted scattered T-cell lymphocytes and a CD138 stain highlighted scattered plasma cells (Figure 5A-C). Staining was negative for CD30, Pax5, EMA, Alk-1, CD21, and CD23. FISH studies were negative for MDM2 amplification. She also underwent aneurysm repair and histology demonstrated periaortic chronic inflammation (Figure 6). The biopsy ruled out malignancy but with the presence of chronic inflammation on pathology, there was a suspicion for idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis. She was referred to the rheumatology clinic for further evaluation.

plate_findings.evidence: Caption: 'Pathology demonstrated dense fibrous tissue with lymphoid plasma cell infiltration'; in-text: 'diffuse proliferation of collagen fibers'

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (a, b, c). a: H&E of retroperitoneal fibrous tissue from a confirmed idiopathic RPF case showing dense collagenous (storiform) fibrosis with lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate, the classic histologic manifestation of retroperitoneal fibrosis. b: IgG4 immunohistochemistry of the same patient's retroperitoneal fibrous tissue; the caption explicitly states the infiltrated plasma cells were IgG4 negative, supporting idiopathic (IgG4-negative) RPF. Real patient histopathology of the disease; the IgG4-positive vocabulary finding is deliberately not tagged because the stain is negative. c: IgG4 immunostain (negative, blue only) of the retroperitoneal fibrous tissue confirming IgG4-negative plasma cells, consistent with idiopathic RPF. Real patient histopathology of the disease; the IgG4-positive vocabulary finding is not tagged because the stain is negative.

The caption, in-text mention and disease-focused title all attribute the finding to retroperitoneal fibrosis, matching the vocabulary finding retroperitoneal_fibrosis_retroperitoneal_fdg_uptake. No age or ethnicity is stated; no skin is shown.

in_text_mentions: A ureteric stent was placed to relieve the obstruction after which there was a resolution of the hydronephrosis and hydroureter. She was discharged and later followed-up with the oncology clinic for evaluation of the mass. A positron-emission tomography (PET) scan was obtained that demonstrated a moderately hypermetabolic soft tissue mass encasing the distal left ureter (Figure 3). A surgical biopsy of the retroperitoneal mass was scheduled but was delayed due to the COVID-19 pandemic.

panels.rationale: Single axial contrast-enhanced CT (arterial phase) from a disease-focused case report of postpartum retroperitoneal fibrosis with IVC obstruction. The panel is a real patient image showing two specific RPF manifestations: IVC obstruction with compensatory gonadal-vein collateral flow (blue arrow) and right obstructive hydronephrosis/hydroureter (red arrow), matching the configured findings vocabulary. Postpartum onset with IVC obstruction and unilateral (right) hydronephrosis is a recognized less-common presentation rather than the classic bilateral periaortic plaque picture, hence variant. No skin is shown, and neither caption nor in-text states age or ethnicity. [raw subtype: postpartum]
panels.attribution_text: Basiimwa et al. Postpartum Retroperitoneal Fibrosis With IVC Obstruction: A Case Report.. Case reports in radiology 2026. doi:10.1155/crra/6285423. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 5.
panels.figure_caption: Axial econtrasted‐enhacned CT image in arterial phase showing the left gonadal vein (blue arrow) opacified in an arterial enhancement pattern showing collateral flow in the presence of IVC obstruction. There is hydronephrosis and hydroureter of the right kidney (red arrow).
in_text_mentions: tified (Figure 2), with compensatory collateral venous return through extensive pelvic varices draining via the gonadal veins (Figures 3 and 4) into the left renal vein and the suprarenal IVC (Figure 5). Right ureteral obstruction with resultant hydronephrosis and hydroureter was also present (Figure 5). panels.rationale: Single axial enhanced abdominal CT image from a case report of IgG4-related focal retroperitoneal fibrosis. The caption and in-text mention describe a 30-mm soft-tissue mass involving the left ureter anterior to the left common iliac artery bifurcation, matching the visible soft-tissue lesion indicated by the arrow adjacent to the contrast-filled iliac vessels. The article title is disease-focused (IgG4-related focal retroperitoneal fibrosis) and the captioned manifestation is specific, supporting attribution to retroperitoneal fibrosis. The focal, unilateral, non-hydronephrotic presentation is a recognized less common (variant) form. No hydronephrosis is present per the caption, and the image is a real patient CT with an arrow annotation. [raw subtype: IgG4-related]
panels.attribution_text: Ueki et al. IgG4-related focal retroperitoneal fibrosis in ureter suggestive of colon cancer recurrence and resected laparoscopically: a case report.. Surgical case reports 2020. doi:10.1186/s40792-020-00964-0. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Enhanced abdominal computed tomography (CT) findings. Enhanced abdominal CT showed a 30-mm soft-tissue mass involving the left ureter in front of the bifurcation of the left common iliac artery (arrow)
in_text_mentions: CT showed a 30-mm soft-tissue mass involving the left ureter in front of the bifurcation of the left common iliac artery but no enlarged lymph nodes, hydronephrosis, or other abnormal findings (Fig. 1). The mass had grown from 16.7 × 10.3 mm to 30 × 13.7 mm in 17 months. Fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography CT (PET-CT) showed significant accumulation of FDG uptake in the same region (maximum standardized uptake value, 8.93; Fig. 2). Significant FDG uptake was not observed at any of the other sites. Ureterography and colonoscopy showed no abnormal findings. Fig. 1E

panels.rationale: Single coronal contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis from a real patient (annotated with a green oval and an 'R' marker). The caption and in-text describe an ill-defined retroperitoneal soft-tissue mass extending from the renal hilum to the aortic bifurcation and encasing the mid-ureter, with the radiology explicitly judged most consistent with retroperitoneal fibrosis (RPF). This supports a periaortic/infrarenal retroperitoneal fibrotic plaque. Disease attribution is strong (in-text states the appearances were most consistent with RPF), though tissue diagnosis was not obtained and the mass is right-predominant with unilateral mid-ureter encasement rather than the classic symmetric bilateral medial ureteral deviation, hence variant typicality and high-but-not-maximal confidence.

panels.figure_caption: Imaging findings of retroperitoneal fibrosis with peripancreatic and hepatic involvement of the patient. (A,B) Abdominal contrast-enhanced CT revealed duodenal compression by a congenitally enlarged pancreatic head, stricture of the hepatic portal bile duct, and dilation of second- and third-order bile ducts on the right. The bile duct wall appeared thickened with contrast enhancement. (C–E) Coronal and sagittal contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated thickening and enhancement of the bile duct wall. Space-occupying lesions in the retroperitoneal and peripancreatic regions extended toward the round ligament of the liver, exhibiting a fibrosis-like appearance rather than a well-defined mass.
in_text_mentions: d, stricture of the hepatic portal bile duct, dilation of the level-two and level-three bile ducts on the right side, and thickening with enhancement of the bile duct wall were also confirmed. Contrast-enhanced CT and repeated MRCP upon referral revealed duodenal compression by an enlarged pancreatic head, hepatic bile duct strictures, and thickened, enhancing bile duct walls suggestive of obstruction (Figure 1). PET-CT demonstrated only mildly elevated metabolic activity in lesions around the ligamentum teres hepatis, which was not sufficient to establish a definitive diagnosis of malignancy.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Human-patient CTA 3D reconstruction. The caption and article title explicitly attribute the infrarenal/aortoiliac aortic occlusion to retroperitoneal fibrosis, so disease attribution is supported rather than inferred from a complication alone. The visualized manifestation is the occlusion with non-opacified collateral/bypass graft, a less common (variant) presentation of RBF. B: Axial contrast CT cross-section in a 65-year-old man showing the occluded infrarenal aorta encased by a dense periaortic mass that the caption describes as typical of retroperitoneal fibrosis — the textbook periaortic fibro-inflammatory mass (classic presentation). Human patient image, clear quality, arrow annotation present.
panels.attribution_text: Wang et al. Thoracobifemoral bypass for infrarenal aortic occlusion caused by retroperitoneal fibrosis.. Journal of vascular surgery cases and innovative techniques 2022. doi:10.1016/j.jvscit.2022.01.005. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Computed tomographic angiography (CTA) in a 65-year-old man with retroperitoneal fibrosis (RBF) and aortic occlusion. panels.rationale: Single axial contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis from a case report titled on retroperitoneal fibrosis. The caption and in-text explicitly document right ureteric encasement with moderate right hydronephrosis, a classic CT manifestation of retroperitoneal fibrosis, and the prior caption triage confirmed a real patient radiology image of the target disease. A blue arrow annotates the encased right ureter/retroperitoneal soft tissue. Captioned colon and gallbladder thickening are listed only as proposed findings since they are not in the vocabulary and their disease association is unclear.

plate_findings.evidence: caption: dense collagenous bands of fibrous tissue encircling the lobules of omental fat

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Real patient H&E section from an omental/peritoneal biopsy in an ergotamine-induced retroperitoneal fibrosis article; shows dense collagenous fibrous bands encircling omental fat, a textbook histologic manifestation of retroperitoneal fibrosis (storiform/dense sclerotic fibrosis). [raw subtype: ergotamine_induced] B: Real patient H&E section showing acellular collagen replacing omental fat (old scar), the inactive/collagenised phase of the same retroperitoneal fibroinflammatory process described in the article and caption; consistent with storiform/dense sclerotic fibrosis of retroperitoneal fibrosis. [raw subtype: ergotamine_induced] C: Real patient Masson Trichrome section with blue collagen deposition highlighting the omental fibroinflammatory process at a different stage of evolution; same ergotamine-induced retroperitoneal fibrosis biopsy, demonstrating the collagenous fibrosis component. [raw subtype: ergotamine_induced]
panels.attribution_text: Patra et al. Ergotamine Induced Retroperitoneal Fibrosis.. Mediterranean journal of rheumatology 2021. doi:10.31138/mjr.32.2.168. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Haematoxylin eosin stained multiple sections from the omental and peritoneal biopsy showing dense collagenous bands of fibrous tissue encircling the lobules of omental fat (A); and at places, with deposition of acellular collagen completely replacing the fat representing old scar (B) (original magnification, x200). Note, the omental fibroinflammatory process at different stages of evolution being highlighted by Masson Trichrome stain (blue) (C, original magnification, x200).

in_text_mentions: flat, soft abdomen with normal bowel sounds and no palpable masses, but with diffuse tenderness across the lower abdomen, especially in the right lower quadrant and suprapubic region. The patient underwent a non-contrast CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with findings significant for an extensive, predominantly right-sided retroperitoneal mass encircling the aorta, inferior vena cava (Figure 1), and proximal right ureter, producing severe obstructive uropathy of the right kidney with massive distention of the pyelocaliceal system and proximal ureter and marked loss of renal cortex (Figure 2).

The patient underwent right ureteral stent placement, which partially resolved hydronephrosis and restored kidney function. The CT-guided biopsy of the retroperitoneal mass revealed fibro-inflammatory tissue without specific features (Figure 2). The immunohistochemistry staining was notable for IgG4-positive plasma cells and CD68-positive histiocytes (Figure 3).

plate_findings.evidence: healed vasculitis with fibrosis replacing the muscle fibre; storiform collagenous fibrosis (visual)

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: H&E section from the ergotamine-induced retroperitoneal fibrosis article; the black arrow indicates fibrinoid necrosis of a small arteriolar wall and the asterisk extravasated red blood cells. Active small-vessel vasculitis is not a vocabulary key, so those specific vascular terms are proposed. B: H&E section in the same retroperitoneal fibrosis specimen showing healed vasculitis with fibrosis replacing the arteriolar muscle fibre; the fibrotic component is mapped to the RPF storiform-fibrosis vocabulary, while the healed-vasculitis terms are proposed. C: Masson Trichrome panel of the same lesion highlights collagenous fibrosis associated with healed arteriolar vasculitis; it is a real histopathology panel of the ergotamine-induced retroperitoneal fibrosis case, not a diagram or other-disease panel. D: Verhoeff-Van Gieson panel of the same retroperitoneal fibrosis specimen highlights elastic/fibrous change of healed vasculitis; it is...
panels.attribution_text: Patra et al. Ergotamine Induced Retroperitoneal Fibrosis.. Mediterranean journal of rheumatology 2021. doi:10.31138/mjr.32.2.168. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 4.
panels.figure_caption: Hematoxylin eosin stained sections highlighting small vessel vasculitis involving arterioles characterized by fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel wall (black arrow) and extravasated red blood cells (black asterisk) (A, x400). Old haemorrhage with hemosiderin laden macrophages were also evident (not shown in the figure). Also note the evidence of healed vasculitis with fibrosis replacing the muscle fibre (B, x400) as highlighted on Masson Trichrome (C, x400) and Verhoeff-Van Gieson (D, x400) stain.
in_text_mentions: atory infiltrate comprised mainly of CD3+, CD4+ small mature T lymphocytes admixed with few CD20+ B cells. Also, the infiltrating plasma cells were negative for IgG4 monoclonal antibody. The vascular changes ranged from active vasculitis with transmural fibrinoid necrosis to obliterative vasculopathy; whereas healed vasculitis and creeping fibrosis into the vessel wall were more commonly observed in medium sized arterioles (better highlighted by Masson Trichrome and Verhoeff-Van Gieson [VVG] stain) (Figure 4A,B,C,D). Foci of old haemorrhage with collection of haemosiderophages were also noted.

panels.rationale: Single axial contrast CT of the abdomen from a human patient. The caption and in-text explicitly state the radiologist recognized circumferential periaortic and proximal right common iliac soft-tissue thickening as retroperitoneal fibrosis at diagnosis, and the article title identifies idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis. The yellow arrow marks the periaortic/iliac soft-tissue plaque. The caption explicitly excludes hydronephrosis and ureteral deviation, so those findings are not tagged. The article title labels the presentation as atypical (initially misdiagnosed as lymphoma), so typicality is atypical. [raw subtype: idiopathic]

panels.figure_caption: Repeat CT at the time of diagnosis. Circumferential soft tissue thickening around the distal abdominal aorta and proximal right common iliac measuring up to 1 cm in thickness (arrow). There is no appreciable hydronephrosis or ureteral displacement.
in_text_mentions: The diagnosis of lymphoma was doubted by the oncologist. On physical exam, there was no palpable lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Repeat CT scan again revealed circumferential soft tissue thickening around the distal abdominal aorta and proximal right common iliac artery but, this time, the radiologist recognized that the findings were more consistent with retroperitoneal fibrosis (Figure 2).

panels.rationale: Single axial abdominal MRI from a human patient with idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis (article title and prior triage confirm real patient image, no third-party issue). The yellow arrow and crosshair localize circumferential soft-tissue thickening encasing the infrarenal aorta, the classic periaortic fibrotic plaque of RPF. The caption explicitly notes absent ureteral retraction and no hydronephrosis, and the article title labels this an atypical presentation, so typicality is atypical. No age, ethnicity, or skin is shown. The in-text 'mild T2 hyperenhancement' is not represented in the vocabulary and is listed as a proposed finding rather than forced into the low-T2 (inactive) category. [raw subtype: idiopathic]

panels.body_site: retroperitoneum (periaortic soft-tissue encasement of the infrarenal abdominal aorta)
panels.rationale: Single axial contrast CT of the abdomen in a human patient from a case report titled 'Atypical Presentation of Idiopathic Retroperitoneal Fibrosis Effectively Treated With Colchicine After Lymphoma Misdiagnosis.' The yellow arrow marks a periaortic infiltrating soft-tissue mass encasing the infrarenal abdominal aorta with mildly reactive lymph nodes — the characteristic radiologic manifestation of retroperitoneal fibrosis, which the patient actually had despite the initial lymphoma interpretation stated in the caption. The panel-specific manifestation (periaortic infiltrating mass) plus the disease-focused article title support attribution to idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis rather than lymphoma; the caption's lymphoma reference reflects the initial misdiagnosis discussed in the article, and the caption itself details features arguing against lymphoma (non-confluent nodes, no anterior aortic displacement, intact bones, no psoas dislocation). The periaortic fibrotic plaque maps directly to a vocabulary finding; mildly reactive lymph nodes are additionally proposed. The article title explicitly labels the presentation as atypical, and the caption's atypical features (absence of anterior aortic displacement) support typicality=atypical. No age or ethnicity is stated; no skin is visible, so skin_tone is null. [raw subtype: idiopathic]
panels.attribution_text: Altshuler. Atypical Presentation of Idiopathic Retroperitoneal Fibrosis Effectively Treated With Colchicine After Lymphoma Misdiagnosis.. Cureus 2021. doi:10.7759/cureus.14756. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: CT that was used to diagnose lymphoma. Visible is a periaortic infiltrating mass (arrow) and mildly reactive lymph nodes. Note that lymph nodes are non-confluent, the aorta is not displaced anteriorly, the bones are intact, and there is no psoas muscle dislocation.
in_text_mentions: ous vomiting and endorsed tingling in the lower extremities but denied dysuria. Of note, the patient reported taking Cafergot (ergotamine tartrate and caffeine) for migraines for several months about a decade prior to presentation. He was a former smoker with 25 pack-years who had quit 10 years prior to admission. CT imaging revealed a periaortic infiltrating mass involving the infrarenal abdominal aorta with mildly prominent lymph nodes thought to represent a malignancy (Figure 1). The mass was not amenable to percutaneous biopsy. The patient was told he had lymphoma and referred to oncology.
